title: The Future Seen from the Past
summary: Describe plans, predictions and expectations as future relative to a past moment. Choose appropriate past-viewpoint forms, distinguish expected and actual outcomes, and interpret formal was or were to constructions for eventual events and unrealised arrangements.
learningObjectives: Shift will, be going to, present-continuous plans and other future expressions to forms appropriate to a past narrative or report.
Distinguish what someone expected at an earlier point from what eventually happened, without assuming that every intention was fulfilled.
Recognise past-viewpoint arrangements, future perfects, imminent actions and the possible overlap with present-tense reporting when the event is still future.
Differentiate retrospective was or were to + infinitive from was or were to have + past participle and choose informal was supposed to where suitable.

explanation.heading: Move the viewpoint back: would and was going to
explanation.body: An event can be in the future relative to a past point even if it is already in the past for today’s speaker. To report an earlier prediction or intention, will commonly becomes would and am or is going to becomes was going to. These forms express the earlier viewpoint; whether the event actually occurred must come from later context or explicit information.
explanation.example: Mina said in January that she would apply for the scholarship in March, but she later changed her mind.

explanation.heading: Earlier arrangements and events in progress
explanation.body: Past continuous can express arrangements that were still ahead at a past reference time: was meeting, were travelling. Future continuous and future perfect can similarly become would be + -ing and would have + past participle. Keep the relative time markers clear: by Friday or later that evening is measured from the past speaker’s original viewpoint.
explanation.example: We expected that by the following Monday the volunteers would have finished preparing the room.

explanation.heading: Formal arrangements, imminence and overlapping viewpoints
explanation.body: Was or were to + infinitive can report an official arrangement that was future from the earlier viewpoint; was or were about to + infinitive describes something imminent at that past moment. If a reported future event has not yet happened as the speaker talks now, both an original present-or-future form and a backshifted past form may sometimes be valid. Choose the version that makes the time viewpoint easiest to follow.
explanation.example: The organisers announced this morning that the awards ceremony is to take place next week.

explanation.heading: Past plans are not automatically completed actions
explanation.body: A past form such as was going to, was meeting or was about to does not by itself prove the event occurred. A later clause can confirm or cancel it. Statements about reported intentions should not be rewritten as statements of fact without evidence. Sometimes was meeting in a story introduces the plan, while a later clause tells us the actual meeting was cancelled.
explanation.example: I was meeting the curator after lunch, but her train was delayed and we postponed the appointment.

explanation.heading: Retrospective outcomes and plans that never happened
explanation.body: In retrospective narration, was or were to + infinitive can highlight an event that did eventually happen, sometimes with a sense of destiny or hindsight. Was or were to have + past participle instead typically presents an arrangement or expectation that did not materialise. More conversationally, was supposed to often expresses an unrealised plan or obligation. Since was to can also describe an arrangement before its outcome is known, use the surrounding context to establish whether the event occurred.
explanation.example: The young composer was to win several international awards; an earlier competition was to have taken place in April, but it was cancelled.

comparisons.title: A prior intention versus a confirmed later event

left.label: Intention only
left.example: Tomas was going to take the early train.
left.note: The past intention does not tell us whether Tomas travelled.

right.label: Completed event
right.note: The past simple asserts that the journey happened.

comparisons.title: Later reality versus an unrealised arrangement

left.label: Retrospective outcome
left.example: She was to become the gallery’s director five years later.
left.note: The narrator knows that the later appointment actually took place.

right.label: Unrealised plan
right.example: She was to have spoken at the opening, but illness kept her away.
right.note: Was to have spoken describes a planned contribution that did not happen.

examples.sentence: The journalist expected that the investigation would reveal new details.
examples.note: Would reveal presents a prediction about a later event from a past standpoint.

examples.sentence: I was going to call the caretaker, but the missing key turned up first.
examples.note: Was going to expresses an intention that did not need to be carried out.

examples.sentence: At the time, we thought the team would be travelling through the mountains in August.
examples.note: Would be travelling preserves the projected activity in a past expectation.

examples.sentence: The chair announced that the committee was to meet again the following Tuesday.
examples.note: Was to meet reports an official future arrangement from an earlier viewpoint.

examples.sentence: The new library was to have opened in February, but building work continued into April.
examples.note: Was to have opened describes an unrealised scheduled opening.

commonMistakes.incorrect: In January, I thought the report will arrive in February.
commonMistakes.correct: In January, I thought the report would arrive in February.
commonMistakes.why: Would normally reports a future prediction from a past perspective.

commonMistakes.incorrect: She was going submit an application the next morning.
commonMistakes.correct: She was going to submit an application the next morning.
commonMistakes.why: Past-viewpoint be going to requires the infinitive marker to.

commonMistakes.incorrect: He was about leave when the office telephone rang.
commonMistakes.correct: He was about to leave when the office telephone rang.
commonMistakes.why: The past imminent-action construction is was about to + infinitive.

commonMistakes.incorrect: The conference was to held in June, but it was postponed.
commonMistakes.correct: The conference was to have been held in June, but it was postponed.
commonMistakes.why: Was to have been held expresses the unrealised passive plan and fits the explicit postponement.

studyTips: Retell a prediction from last year using would, then add an independent sentence saying whether the prediction came true.
Draw two timelines: one for a past intention that went ahead and another for a past intention that was cancelled; compare their verb forms.
Compare a historical was to become sentence with a cancelled was to have become sentence, and explain why the narrator knows the different outcomes.

exercises.prompt: Last autumn, Ava expected an announcement the following week. Choose the accurate past-viewpoint report.
choices: Ava thought the announcement would come the following week.
Ava thought the announcement will comes the following week.
Ava thought the announcement is coming the previous week.
exercises.feedback: Would come locates the expected announcement in the future relative to Ava’s past expectation.

exercises.prompt: The project was scheduled to start in May, but the sponsors withdrew. Choose the form that highlights an unrealised formal arrangement.
choices: The project was to starting in May.
The project was to have started in May.
The project is to start in May and finished already.
exercises.feedback: Was to have started presents a planned event that did not take place as arranged.

exercises.prompt: A caller nearly left the office when a parcel arrived. Which sentence describes that past moment?
choices: The caller was about leaving when the parcel arrived.
The caller is about to leave when the parcel arrived.
The caller was about to leave when the parcel arrived.
exercises.feedback: Was about to leave expresses an action imminent at the arrival time.

exercises.prompt: Choose the sentence that unambiguously asserts a completed event rather than just an earlier plan.
choices: They were going to tour the castle.
They toured the castle.
They were planning to tour the castle.
exercises.feedback: Toured asserts the visit took place; the planning forms do not.

exercises.prompt: In February, I expected the new course ___ (will / begin) in April. Write the two-word past-viewpoint future phrase.
exercises.feedback: Would begin reports the future relative to the earlier expectation.

exercises.prompt: Her original intention changed. “She ___ (going / rent) a flat, but she stayed with relatives instead.” Write the complete past be going to phrase.
exercises.feedback: Was going to rent describes an intention that the later clause shows did not happen.

exercises.prompt: The opening was planned for March but cancelled. “The gallery ___ (to / open) in March.” Use the four-word unrealised was to have construction.
exercises.feedback: Was to have opened marks a scheduled opening that failed to occur.

exercises.prompt: I was one moment from sending the message. “I ___ (about / send) the message when the power failed.” Write the complete four-word phrase.
exercises.feedback: Was about to send describes an action imminent at a past point.

exercises.prompt: Correct the past prediction: “They believed the visitors will arrive later that evening.”
acceptedAnswers: They believed the visitors would arrive later that evening.
exercises.feedback: Would arrive reports what was future at the time of their belief.

exercises.prompt: Correct using the past continuous arrangement: “We were meet the architect on Thursday, but she cancelled.”
acceptedAnswers: We were meeting the architect on Thursday, but she cancelled.
exercises.feedback: Were meeting expresses the arranged appointment from the earlier viewpoint.

exercises.prompt: Correct the earlier intention: “He was going apply for the grant, but the deadline passed.”
acceptedAnswers: He was going to apply for the grant, but the deadline passed.
exercises.feedback: Going to + infinitive is necessary for the earlier intention.

exercises.prompt: Correct the unfulfilled formal plan: “The gallery was to have open in spring, but repairs caused a delay.”
acceptedAnswers: The gallery was to have opened in spring, but repairs caused a delay.
exercises.feedback: Was to have requires the past participle opened.

speakingExercises.prompt: Report a prediction made last month. Facts: They / think / the prices / rise. Begin “They thought” and use would.
acceptedAnswers: They thought the prices would rise.
speakingExercises.feedback: Would rise gives future relative to their earlier thought.

speakingExercises.prompt: Describe a former intention. Facts: I / going to / study / architecture. Use was going to with a full form.
acceptedAnswers: I was going to study architecture.
speakingExercises.feedback: Was going to study reports what was intended in the past.

speakingExercises.prompt: State an earlier appointment. Facts: We / meet / the editor / on Friday. Use the past continuous.
acceptedAnswers: We were meeting the editor on Friday.
speakingExercises.feedback: Were meeting expresses a planned future event seen from the past.

speakingExercises.prompt: State a past near-action. Facts: She / about to / lock / the door. Use was.
acceptedAnswers: She was about to lock the door.
speakingExercises.feedback: Was about to lock places an imminent action in the past.

speakingExercises.prompt: Describe an unrealised formal arrangement. Facts: The bridge / open / in June / but it was delayed. Use was to have opened.
acceptedAnswers: The bridge was to have opened in June, but it was delayed.
speakingExercises.feedback: Was to have opened identifies the unfulfilled opening plan.

speakingExercises.prompt: Give a retrospective outcome. Facts: The writer / become / famous / years later. Use was to become.
acceptedAnswers: The writer was to become famous years later.
speakingExercises.feedback: Was to become is retrospective narration of a later real outcome.

speakingExercises.prompt: Correct aloud: “I thought the lecture will finish by noon.”
acceptedAnswers: I thought the lecture would finish by noon.
speakingExercises.feedback: Would finish is the backshifted future seen from the past.

speakingExercises.prompt: Say two sentences in this order with full forms. Earlier intention: We / going to / visit the gallery. Cancellation: The gallery / close / unexpectedly. Use past simple for the second sentence.
acceptedAnswers: We were going to visit the gallery. The gallery closed unexpectedly.
speakingExercises.feedback: Were going to visit expresses the plan; closed reports the event that changed it.

listeningExercises.audioText: Last December, the director said that the new studio would open in March. The construction was delayed, and the opening has now been moved to July.
listeningExercises.prompt: Did the studio open in March as predicted?
choices: Yes, and a second one opened in July.
No, its opening was delayed until July.
The studio was demolished in March.
listeningExercises.feedback: Would open reports the past prediction; the later clause explicitly says it did not happen on time.

listeningExercises.audioText: I was about to leave the rehearsal room when the conductor asked everyone to stay for one final piece.
listeningExercises.prompt: What was the speaker on the point of doing?
choices: Calling the conductor.
Starting another rehearsal.
Leaving the rehearsal room.
listeningExercises.feedback: Was about to leave identifies the action that was imminent.

listeningExercises.audioText: The exhibition was to have opened in August, but the organisers cancelled the launch after the flood.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the four-word verb phrase immediately after “exhibition”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Was to have opened is the exact audible phrase; the opening did not happen as planned.

listeningExercises.audioText: When he was a student, the architect produced several sketches. He was to design the city’s most famous concert hall twenty years later.
listeningExercises.prompt: What does the narrator tell us about the architect?
choices: He eventually designed the concert hall.
He was forbidden to design the hall.
His sketches were all destroyed immediately.
listeningExercises.feedback: Was to design is retrospective narration of the later actual achievement.

listeningExercises.audioText: We were meeting our former supervisor the following morning, but she became ill overnight, so we cancelled the visit.
choices: Yes, at the original time.
No, it was cancelled.
Yes, but only on the telephone.
listeningExercises.feedback: Were meeting reports an arrangement; the rest of the audio explicitly says it was cancelled.

listeningExercises.audioText: The committee announced today that the new regulations are to take effect next month. They have not started yet, and nothing has changed this week.
listeningExercises.prompt: When are the regulations expected to take effect?
choices: Earlier today.
Last month.
Next month.
listeningExercises.feedback: Are to take effect is a present-viewpoint report of a future event still ahead.

listeningExercises.audioText: We believed the researchers would have completed the survey by the end of the term.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the three-word projected perfect phrase immediately after “researchers”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Would have completed places the predicted completion before a later deadline from a past viewpoint.

listeningExercises.audioText: Our group was going to visit the archive, but the building had to close for repairs.
listeningExercises.prompt: Type the four-word past-intention phrase immediately after “group”.
listeningExercises.feedback: Was going to visit expresses a previous intention, which the closure disrupted.
